senses: a gap, a crack, a space between
between, among; an interval of time
(jiàn) to separate, to come between; a spy
間.shuowenEn: A crack. From gate and moon. (The Shuowen enters the older form 閒, with the moon; 間, with the sun, is the later graph.)

parts.m: sun (in the older form 月, moon)

間.story: Light seen between the leaves of a shut gate: moonlight in the older form, sunlight in the later one. From the crack came each kind of between, in space and in time. In passage 5 the space 間 heaven and earth is like a bellows. In passage 43, that which has no substance enters 無間, where there is no gap. The moon form 閒 was kept for “leisure”.
間.gap: English uses many words: gap, interval, room, between. 間 holds them as one idea, an opening with something at each side.

senses: the utmost, the furthest point; most
solstice (the sun’s arrival at its limit)
至.shuowen: 鳥飛从高下至地也。从一，一猶地也。象形。
至.shuowenEn: A bird flies from on high down to the ground. From 一, and the 一 is like the earth. A picture.
至.story: The Shuowen sees a bird that lands; many modern scholars see an arrow that has struck the ground. From arrival comes the limit, and 至 before a word makes it “the most”: the softest and the hardest under heaven (43), the height of harmony in the infant (55). As a verb: push emptiness to its limit, 致虛極, uses the related 致 (16).
至.gap: “Most” and “utmost” are only grammar in English. 至 still has a flight and a landing in it.

senses: to drive horses hard; to gallop, to race
to spread fast (of fame, of thought)
馳.shuowenEn: To drive hard. From 馬 (horse), with 也 for the sound.
馳.story: A horse at speed. With 騁 it makes the set phrase 馳騁, a full gallop in the hunt or in war. The Laozi uses the phrase two times, with opposite values: the gallop and the hunt drive the heart mad (12); the softest thing under heaven gallops over the hardest (43). The short form is 驰.
馳.gap: “Overcomes” and “penetrates”, common in English versions, lose the animal.

senses: to give free rein to (the eye, the mind)
騁.shuowenEn: To race straight ahead. From 馬 (horse), with 甹 for the sound.
騁.story: The partner of 馳: a run at full stretch with no turn. Later writers use it for the eye that ranges over a view and the mind that runs free. In the Laozi it occurs only in the pair 馳騁 (12, 43).
騁.gap: None in the word. English has “gallop” for both 馳 and 騁 and so cannot double the verb as the Chinese does.

senses: strong (of armor, walls); to make firm
堅.shuowenEn: Hard. From 臤 and 土 (earth).

parts.m: firm, tight; the Shuowen glosses it with 堅 itself

堅.story: Hardness as of packed earth. In the Laozi it is the mark of death and of that which loses. People are soft and weak at birth and 堅 and stiff at death; the hard and strong are followers of death (76). Nothing is better than water at attacking the 堅 (78). The softest gallops over the most 堅 (43).
堅.gap: “Firm” is praise in English. In the Laozi 堅 is a warning.

senses: to reach, to catch up with
to come to, to extend to
及.shuowenEn: To catch up with. From a hand and a person.

parts.m: a hand that reaches from behind

及.story: A hand takes hold of a person from behind. The wordless teaching and the gain of not-doing are things that few in the world 及 (43). The great trouble that I have is that I have a self; if I had none, what trouble would 及, reach, me (13)?
及.gap: “Attain” sounds like an achievement. 及 is plainer: to come level with someone on the road.

入.shuowenEn: To go inside. It shows things that come down together from above.
入.story: Two strokes that lean together and point up, like a wedge or a root tip. Its partner is 出, to come out. The Laozi pairs them for birth and death: 出生入死, “to come out is life, to go in is death” (50). In passage 43, that which has no substance 入, enters, where there is no gap.
